issues.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession unless it is accompanied by an open, continuous, hostile possession and a positive intention to dispossess the owner.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that they had possessed the land for more than fifty years and had exercised ownership rights over it.
Their possession followed purchases of land, including land previously conveyed to another claimant.
The claimants’ own evidence indicated that they learned of the other claimant’s rights only when their possession was challenged.
The Court found that the circumstances showed possession and an intention to possess, but did not establish the required positive intention to dispossess.
issues.conclusion: Long possession alone was insufficient; the claimant must establish an intention to dispossess that is openly manifested and gives the owner reasonable notice and an opportunity to object.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of adverse possession requires a two-pronged inquiry: the limitation period must have run against the owner, and the possessor must have a positive intention to dispossess the owner. Intention to possess is not a substitute for intention to dispossess. Possession must be peaceful, open, continuous, exclusive, and hostile, in the sense of being sufficiently evident to give the owner reasonable notice. The Court relied on Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and on Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Saroop Singh v. Banto, Thakur Kishan Singh v. Arvind Kumar, and Powell v. Macfarlane.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and possession_is_long and (intent_to_possess_only or hostile_intent_not_openly_manifested)

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A possessor claims that possession has extinguished another person’s title and vested title in the possessor.
predicates.possession_is_long: The possessor has occupied or used the property for a lengthy period.
predicates.intent_to_possess_only: The possessor’s conduct shows an intention to occupy or use the property but does not show an intention to exclude the owner.
predicates.hostile_intent_not_openly_manifested: The possessor has not made an intention to exclude the owner sufficiently open and evident to give the owner reasonable notice.

issues.definition: When a person claims title through adverse possession, lengthy occupation does not establish that title if the conduct shows only an intention to possess or fails to openly manifest an intention to dispossess the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant asserting title by adverse possession must plead and prove when possession became adverse, the nature and extent of that possession, and facts showing that it was hostile to the identified owner.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that their possession had been open, continuous, uninterrupted, and hostile for more than fifty years.
Their pleadings and evidence did not disclose when their possession became adverse or adequately set out how it became open, continuous, and hostile.
The claimants’ asserted possession followed conveyances, one of which concerned land previously conveyed to another claimant.
The claimants had established no evidentiary basis for identifying a starting point from which adverse possession could be measured.
issues.conclusion: The claimants had not pleaded and proved the facts necessary to establish adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: A plea of adverse possession is a mixed question of fact and law. The claimant must clearly plead and prove the starting point of adverse possession, the nature of possession, whether it was known to the owner, its duration, and whether it was open and undisturbed; the true owner must also be identified. Under Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, once the opposing party establishes title, the burden of proving adverse possession lies on the claimant. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Saroop Singh v. Banto, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, and Narne Rama Murthy v. Ravula Somasundaram. It contrasted this allocation of the burden with Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and (adverse_start_not_pleaded or possession_characteristics_not_proved or true_owner_not_identified)

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A claimant seeks to defeat another person’s title by asserting ownership through possession.
predicates.adverse_start_not_pleaded: The claimant has not pleaded when the possession became hostile to the owner.
predicates.possession_characteristics_not_proved: The claimant has not proved the nature, openness, continuity, extent, or notice of the claimed adverse possession.
predicates.true_owner_not_identified: The claimant has not specifically identified the person whose title the possession is said to have displaced.

issues.definition: A claimant asserting title through adverse possession fails to prove the claim when the claimant omits to plead the starting point, fails to prove the required characteristics of possession, or does not identify the owner whose title is challenged.

issues.legal_issue: Possession following purchases of land did not establish adverse possession where the claimants failed to prove when possession became hostile or that they intended openly to dispossess the prior titleholder.
material_facts: The claimants appealed from a judgment rejecting a decree that had recognized their title by adverse possession.
The claimants took possession after purchases of land, while another claimant had previously acquired part of the land.
The claimants asserted lengthy possession but did not establish when it became adverse or prove the required hostile intention.
The claimants’ evidence indicated that they learned of the other claimant’s rights only when their possession was challenged.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed because the claimants had not established title by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Possession, even when unusually long and undisturbed, does not establish adverse title without the required animus possidendi directed toward dispossessing the owner, manifested through open and hostile conduct, and supported by proof of when the possession became adverse. The Court applied Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Saroop Singh v. Banto, and Thakur Kishan Singh v. Arvind Kumar.

rule.if: appeal_from_reversal_of_adverse_possession_decree and possession_followed_later_purchase and earlier_transfer_to_other_claimant and claimant_learned_of_other_title_only_after_dispute and adverse_start_not_proved and hostile_intent_not_proved

predicates.appeal_from_reversal_of_adverse_possessi: A litigant appeals from a judgment that rejected a decree recognizing the litigant’s claim of title by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_followed_later_purchase: The claimant’s possession of the disputed property followed a purchase or other transaction concerning land.
predicates.earlier_transfer_to_other_claimant: Another claimant had acquired an interest in some of the property before the transaction relied on by the possessor.
predicates.claimant_learned_of_other_title_only_aft: The possessor’s evidence indicates that the possessor learned of the other claimant’s rights only after the possession was challenged.
predicates.adverse_start_not_proved: The claimant does not prove when possession became hostile to the owner.
predicates.hostile_intent_not_proved: The claimant does not prove an openly manifested intention to exclude and dispossess the owner.

issues.definition: An appeal from rejection of an adverse-possession decree is dismissed when possession followed a later purchase despite an earlier transfer to another claimant, the possessor learned of that interest only after a dispute, and the claimant failed to prove when possession became adverse or an openly manifested intention to dispossess.
